title: I Applied the Pickleball Paddle Checkout to the Captain Who Took Our Numbered Set

parts.text: I stepped on court four at 6:04 p.m. and captain Rhea was already serving with our numbered paddles. The board said: ONE COURT. NINETY MINUTES. PADDLES STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-two, league lead, holding a clipboard that listed our slot. Rhea shrugged. "Captains are the court." I photographed the board, the booking, and her serve on our baseline. Then I asked for the paddle log. At 6:12 the rec desk pinged why Rhea's name was on our set. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The rec desk can see Rhea's serve on court four during our booking.

social.video_title: She served with our numbered paddles on our court — Part 1/2
social.description: Pickleball court, a captain on our baseline, a ninety-minute clock she posted. I logged the serve. Would you have asked for the paddle log?

parts.text: Rhea called it warm-up until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the baseline still. The paddles went back to our handles. Rhea ran her own ninety minutes and told the next captain atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word captains use when a booking exists. Court policy now has a second line: CAPTAINS ARE NOT THE COURT. I keep our set on a labeled hook. Rhea brown-bags her jokes. The court finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Captains are not the court — Part 2/2
social.description: Paddle log, numbered set, and a second line on the board. Was warm-up ever our baseline?
